## What changed

**The Diátaxis and `@lat:` conventions now bind.**

A consumer session set up `lat.md/` in a Rails app, wrote 760 lines of flat
documents, added no `@lat:` refs, and passed `lat check`. Nothing it did was
wrong under the rules as written — every rule that would have caught it was
scoped away from where it worked.

- **`require-mode`** — `lat init` scaffolds `tutorials/`, `how-to/`,
  `reference/` and `explanation/` into a fresh tree, each with an index written
  to satisfy its own mode, and stamps `require-mode: true` into the root index.
  A document that declares no mode and sits in no mode directory is then a
  `lat check` error. Opt-in and read from the tree, so an existing project is
  untouched until it adds the line.
- **A code-ref floor** — a tree holding documents that no `@lat:` ref anywhere
  reaches now fails, with a remediation that quotes the root index's own H1 so
  the suggested line pastes in and clears the error. `require-code-mention` was
  the only thing asking for refs and it is opt-in frontmatter; an agent could
  simply not write it, and one did.
- **The instruction prose moved out of upstream's templates.**
  `templates/AGENTS.md` is back to upstream's exact bytes and off the
  allowlist; `templates/skill/SKILL.md` likewise. Their 27 lines now live in
  `templates/fork/conventions.md`, written into a consumer under its own
  `%% lat-fork:begin %%` markers and again as a separate `lat-md-conventions`
  skill. The upstream diff got *smaller* while the instruction got stronger.

The new prose argues rather than instructs, because both reasons that session
gave were reasonable: it read a list of example comment markers as a language
allowlist, and its repository treats comments as untrusted input to an agent.
So the text says an `@lat:` line is a machine directive that such a convention
does not reach, and that the marker is a comment syntax, not an allowlist.
